metadata.title: Exploring how institutional structures shape instructional quality: The roles of teacher education, employment, and development in fostering higher-order thinking skills

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher-reported items and focuses on the United States teacher sample (N = 2,560 teachers). It applies teacher weights from the TALIS 2018 dataset to support representative estimation, and it reports that models incorporate replicate sample weights at the teacher level. The multilevel regression framework accounts for clustering of teachers within schools using 165 school clusters (idschool) and adjusts standard errors accordingly. Missing data are handled via multiple imputation before estimation, and the analysis proceeds with weighted, cluster-aware multilevel models rather than any PV-based achievement scaling.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the TALIS 2018 teacher dataset and analyzed the United States teacher sample. The analytic sample consists of teachers with complete data after applying multiple imputation for missing values; outcomes and predictors are based on teacher-reported items measuring instructional quality for higher-order thinking (critical thinking, knowledge transfer, problem-solving) and institutional/teacher characteristics. Models are estimated with teachers nested within schools (165 school clusters) and incorporate replicate sample weights at the teacher level.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (United States) teacher instructional quality — critical thinking item
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression coefficients (B) with replicate-weighted SEs; Model 1 R-squared = 0.02, Model 2 = 0.04, Model 3 = 0.04, Model 4 = 0.05. Key effects: Gender positive and significant (e.g., Model 4 B = 0.086, p < .001); Educational attainment positive and significant (e.g., Model 4 B = 0.089, p < .001). General pedagogy significant in Models 3–4 (e.g., Model 4 B = 0.083, p < .05). Informal PD: observation visits positive and significant in Model 4 (B = 0.102, p < .01); Informal PD: peer/self-observation and coaching positive and significant in Model 4 (B = 0.059, p < .01). Formal PD variables not significant in Model 4.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (United States) teacher instructional quality the study leveraged Gender, Educational attainment, General pedagogy, Classroom practice, and Informal PD (observation visits) to model Critical thinking (teacher-reported instructional practice), finding that female teachers and higher educational attainment were consistently associated with more critical-thinking instructional practices and that informal, practice-based PD (observation visits and peer/self coaching) showed significant positive effects in Model 4. This indicates that strengthening teacher education breadth and prioritizing collaborative, observation- and coaching-based professional learning may be more effective for promoting critical-thinking instruction than relying on formal course-based PD alone, though the study is correlational and based on teacher self-reports.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (United States) teacher instructional quality — knowledge transfer item
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression coefficients (B) with replicate-weighted SEs; R-squared = 0.01 (Model 1), 0.02 (Model 2), 0.03 (Model 3), 0.04 (Model 4). Key effects: General pedagogy positive and significant across Models 2–4 (e.g., Model 4 B = 0.129, p < .001). Working hours of teacher positive and significant (e.g., Model 3 B = 0.163, p < .001; Model 4 B = 0.128, p < .01). Employment status negative and significant in Model 3 (B = -0.053, p < .05) but not in Model 4. Formal PD: formal qualification programs small but significant in Model 4 (B = 0.079, p < .05). Informal PD: observation visits not significant (B = -0.009, n.s.); Informal PD: peer/self-observation and coaching not significant (B = 0.033, n.s.).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (United States) teacher instructional quality the study leveraged General pedagogy, Working hours of teacher, Employment status, Formal PD (formal qualification programs), and Informal PD (peer/self coaching) to model Knowledge transfer (teacher-reported instructional practice), finding that general pedagogical skills and greater full-time working hours were positively associated with knowledge-transfer instruction while employment status showed only a weak negative association in Model 3 that did not persist in Model 4. This indicates that policies supporting teachers’ sustained instructional time and strengthening general pedagogical preparation may improve knowledge-transfer practices, and that formal qualification PD may help modestly, though causality cannot be inferred from the observational, teacher-reported design.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (United States) teacher instructional quality — problem-solving item
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression coefficients (B) with replicate-weighted SEs; R-squared = 0.00 (Model 1), 0.01 (Model 2), 0.02 (Model 3), 0.04 (Model 4). Key effects: Educational attainment small but significant in Models 1 and 4 (e.g., Model 4 B = 0.039, p < .05). Content of subject negative and significant across Models 2–4 (e.g., Model 4 B = -0.055, p < .05). General pedagogy positive and significant across Models 2–4 (e.g., Model 4 B = 0.064, p < .05). Formal PD: in-person courses and seminars positive and significant in Model 4 (B = 0.164, p < .01); Formal PD: online courses and seminars positive and significant in Model 4 (B = 0.073, p < .05); Formal PD: formal qualification programs positive and significant in Model 4 (B = 0.071, p < .05). Informal PD: observation visits positive and significant in Model 4 (B = 0.082, p < .05); Informal PD: peer/self-observation and coaching positive and significant in Model 4 (B = 0.075, p < .01). Employment status and working hours not significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (United States) teacher instructional quality the study leveraged Educational attainment, Content of subject, General pedagogy, and both formal and informal PD indicators to model Problem-solving (teacher-reported instructional practice), finding that general pedagogy and multiple forms of PD were positively associated with problem-solving instruction while subject content knowledge showed a negative association and employment status/working hours were not significant. This indicates that teacher development strategies should emphasize pedagogical preparation and PD participation (both structured and practice-based) to strengthen problem-solving instruction, while relying on content expertise alone may not translate into better problem-solving teaching, though the results remain correlational and based on self-reported practices.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher-reported instructional quality in the United States (N = 2,560 teachers nested in 165 schools) to examine how institutional structures—teacher education, employment status, and professional development—relate to higher-order thinking practices. Outcomes are three teacher-reported items: critical thinking, knowledge transfer, and problem-solving, modeled using weighted multilevel regression with multiple imputation for missing data. Across models, general pedagogy is a consistent positive predictor for all three instructional domains, while subject content knowledge is not uniformly beneficial (notably negative for problem-solving). Informal PD (observation visits and peer/self coaching) shows significant positive associations with critical thinking, whereas formal PD formats (in-person, online, and qualification programs) show significant positive associations with problem-solving. The study reports R-squared values up to 0.05 and relies on self-reports, so findings indicate associations rather than causal effects.
